steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a human factors paper arguing that showing a human supervisor the automation's command signal haptically (through a manual control interface in their hand) could improve supervisory performance, leading into an experiment comparing no sharing, visual sharing and haptic sharing.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Humans moving from operator to supervisor, and are poor supervisors
- Operator vs. supervisor: access to command u(t)
- Why being in control helps (motion sickness, efference copy / reafference)
- Hypothesis: giving the supervisor a copy of u(t) through a moving manual interface
- Difference from Haptic Shared Control
- Why haptic rather than visual
- This paper: experiment and simulation

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
As automation becomes more capable, humans get promoted from the role of operator to the role of supervisor, and they are often asked to monitor multiple automated agents at the same time. As supervisors, humans are expected to detect automation faults, to intervene when recovery is beyond what the automation can do, and to re-program automation objectives when needed. But humans are notoriously ill-equipped to supervise. Humans lose vigilance when sustained attention is required, and they have difficulty interpreting the visual displays that are conventionally used in supervisory control settings.

If we look at the differences between the roles of operator and supervisor, we see an opportunity to give the supervisor additional information. An operator generates the command signal u(t) that they issue through the manual control interface, and so they have access to it through both efference copy, and proprioception. A supervisor, on the other hand, relies only on visually monitoring the reference signal r(t) and the system output y(t). So the question is, would the control signal u(t) be of any benefit to the supervisor?

It is well known that the operator, the person in the driver's seat, whether literally or figuratively, has a privilege. For example, a driver rarely gets motion sickness like the passengers of the vehicle, and this is precisely because the driver can anticipate visual and/or vestibular cues. The advantage of being in control has been recognized for a long time in human motor behavior. The operator holds an internal model of the system under control and has generated the control command u(t), so the operator can produce an expected sensory feedback signal. Von Holst and Mittelstaedt postulated that higher level control systems only need to be involved when there are discrepancies between expected and actual sensory feedback. Expected sensory feedback can be compared to the sensory input that comes from human movement, which is called reafference, and this makes it possible to shield perception from self-induced effects on the sensory stream. This shielding is critical for stabilizing the sensory field, for example to remove the effects of eye and head movements from the image projected on the retina.

Hypothesis:
- supervisor with copy of u(t) may get same benefits as operator
- manual control interface moved by another agent, in passive hand of supervisor
- better anticipation of y(t); better determination of operator's control intent

Haptic Shared Control:
- control intent matters when sharing control
- displays autonomous agent's command u(t) to driver; driver feels command torque
- but control sharing vs. our supervisory control (information only from agent to supervisor)
- supervisor cannot “edit” u(t); may take over (supervisory role suspended)

Why haptic:
- prior experience as operator may come into play
- more aligned with haptic than visual copy; recognizable as signal they might have issued

This paper:
- experiment: operator's command (“wizarding” automation) not shared / shared visually / shared haptically; participant always supervisor
- simple simulation study first: supervisor/participant as input observer
- brief discussion and future work

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
As automation becomes more capable, humans get promoted from the role of operator to the role of supervisor, and they are often asked to monitor multiple automated agents at the same time. As supervisors, humans are expected to detect automation faults, to intervene when recovery is beyond what the automation can do, and to re-program automation objectives when needed. But humans are notoriously ill-equipped to supervise. Humans lose vigilance when sustained attention is required, and they have difficulty interpreting the visual displays that are conventionally used in supervisory control settings.

If we look at the differences between the roles of operator and supervisor, we see an opportunity to give the supervisor additional information. An operator generates the command signal u(t) that they issue through the manual control interface, and so they have access to it through both efference copy, and proprioception. A supervisor, on the other hand, relies only on visually monitoring the reference signal r(t) and the system output y(t). So the question is, would the control signal u(t) be of any benefit to the supervisor?

It is well known that the operator, the person in the driver's seat, whether literally or figuratively, has a privilege. For example, a driver rarely gets motion sickness like the passengers of the vehicle, and this is precisely because the driver can anticipate visual and/or vestibular cues. The advantage of being in control has been recognized for a long time in human motor behavior. The operator holds an internal model of the system under control and has generated the control command u(t), so the operator can produce an expected sensory feedback signal. Von Holst and Mittelstaedt postulated that higher level control systems only need to be involved when there are discrepancies between expected and actual sensory feedback. Expected sensory feedback can be compared to the sensory input that comes from human movement, which is called reafference, and this makes it possible to shield perception from self-induced effects on the sensory stream. This shielding is critical for stabilizing the sensory field, for example to remove the effects of eye and head movements from the image projected on the retina.

So it seems plausible that if the supervisor has a copy of u(t), the supervisor might also get the same benefits as the operator. We hypothesize that if we place a manual control interface that moves under the action of another agent into the passive hand of a human supervisor, who does not generate the control signal, the supervisor's ability to anticipate the response y(t) will improve. We also hypothesize that the supervisor will be in a better position to determine what the control intent of the operator is.

It is particularly important to determine the control intent of an operator when you share control with another operator. Haptic Shared Control is partly an example of displaying the command u(t) of an autonomous agent so that a human driver has access to it. The driver senses the automation's command torque by feel. However, Haptic Shared Control is fundamentally a paradigm for control sharing, while the paradigm in this paper is supervisory control, where information is transmitted strictly from the autonomous agent to the human supervisor. The supervisor cannot “edit” the automation's command u(t) like in Haptic Shared Control, though the supervisor may choose to take over control from the automation, and then the supervisory role is suspended.

We conjecture that the supervisor's prior experience acting as an operator can come into play when they perceptually process the command signal u(t) that another agent generates. We also expect that this sensorimotor processing will be more aligned with a haptic copy of u(t) than with a visual one. Haptics may have an advantage for supplying the command copy in a form that the supervisor recognizes as a signal they might have issued themselves.

In this paper we describe an experiment that is designed to quantify the merits of giving a copy of an operator's command u(t) to a supervisor/participant. In the experiment, the command of a human operator (“wizarding” an automation system) was either not shared with the participant, shared visually, or shared haptically. In all cases the participant acted as a supervisor. Before we present the experimental methods and results, we describe a simple simulation study where the supervisor/participant is interpreted as an input observer. At the end of the paper there is a brief discussion of results and future work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
As the capabilities of automation advance, humans are promoted from the role of operator to that of supervisor, often being asked to monitor multiple automated agents simultaneously. As supervisors, humans are expected to detect automation faults, to intervene when recovery is beyond automation capabilities, and to re-program automation objectives when necessary. Yet humans are notoriously ill-equipped to supervise [1]. They lose vigilance when sustained attention is required [2] and have difficulty interpreting the visual displays conventionally used in supervisory control settings [3] [4].

When considering the differences between the roles of operator and supervisor, an opportunity to provide the supervisor with additional information becomes apparent. An operator generates, and therefore has access to, the command signal u(t) issued through the manual control interface, by virtue of both efference copy [5], [6] and proprioception. A supervisor, on the other hand, relies strictly on visual monitoring of the reference signal r(t) and system output y(t) [2]. The question arises: would the control signal u(t) be of any benefit to the supervisor?

The privilege afforded the operator (the person in the driver's seat, whether literally or figuratively) is well known. For example, a driver rarely suffers motion sickness like the vehicle's passengers, precisely because the driver can anticipate visual and/or vestibular cues [7]. The advantage of being in control has long been recognized in human motor behavior [8]. By holding an internal model of the system under control and having generated the control command u(t), the operator can produce an expected sensory feedback signal. Von Holst and Mittelstaedt postulated that higher level control systems need to be involved only when discrepancies arise between expected and actual sensory feedback. Expected sensory feedback can be compared to the sensory input resulting from human movement (called reafference) [8], enabling perception to be shielded from self-induced effects on the sensory stream. Such shielding is critical for stabilizing the sensory field, for example in removing the effects of eye and head movements from the image projected on the retina [9].

It seems plausible, then, that if the supervisor has a copy of u(t), the same benefits afforded the operator might also accrue for the supervisor. By placing a manual control interface that moves under the action of another agent into the passive hand of a human supervisor (who does not generate the control signal), we hypothesize that the supervisor's ability to anticipate the response y(t) will improve. We also hypothesize that the supervisor will be in a better position to determine the operator's control intent.

Determining the control intent of an operator is particularly important when sharing control with another operator. Haptic Shared Control [10,11] is in part an example of displaying an autonomous agent's command u(t) to give a human driver access to it: by feel, the driver senses the automation's command torque. However, Haptic Shared Control is fundamentally a paradigm for control sharing, whereas the paradigm we address in this paper is supervisory control, in which information is transmitted strictly from autonomous agent to human supervisor. The supervisor cannot “edit” the automation's command u(t) as in Haptic Shared Control, though the supervisor may choose to take over control from the automation (in which case the supervisory role is suspended).

We conjecture that prior experience acting as an operator can come into play in the supervisor's perceptual processing of a command signal u(t) generated by another agent. Further, we expect such sensorimotor processing to be more aligned with a haptic than with a visual copy of u(t). Haptics may carry an advantage for supplying the command copy in a form the supervisor recognizes as a signal they might themselves have issued.

In this paper we describe an experiment designed to quantify the merits of providing a copy of an operator's command u(t) to a supervisor/participant. In our experiment, the command of a human operator (“wizarding” an automation system) was either not shared with the participant, shared visually, or shared haptically, and the participant acted as a supervisor in all cases. Before presenting the experimental methods and results, we describe a simple simulation study that interprets the supervisor/participant as an input observer. The paper closes with a brief discussion of results and future work.

References:
[1] L. Bainbridge, “Ironies of automation,” in Analysis, design and evaluation of man–machine systems . Elsevier, 1983, pp. 129–135.
[2] T. B. Sheridan, “Human supervisory control,” Handbook of human factors and ergonomics , pp. 990–1015, 2012.
[3] J. Y. Chen, M. J. Barnes, and M. Harper-Sciarini, “Supervisory control of multiple robots: Human-performance issues and user-interface design,” IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, Part C (Applications and Reviews) , vol. 41, no. 4, pp. 435–454, 2010.
[4] T. B. Sheridan, “Human–robot interaction: status and challenges,” Human factors , vol. 58, no. 4, pp. 525–532, 2016.
[5] B. Bridgeman, “Efference copy and its limitations,” Computers in biology and medicine , vol. 37, no. 7, pp. 924–929, 2007.
[6] H. Imamizu, “Prediction of sensorimotor feedback from the efference copy of motor commands: A review of behavioral and functional neuroimaging studies,” Japanese Psychological Research , vol. 52, no. 2, pp. 107–120, 2010.
[7] A. Rolnick and R. Lubow, “Why is the driver rarely motion sick? the role of controllability in motion sickness,” Ergonomics , vol. 34, no. 7, pp. 867–879, 1991.
[8] E. von Holst and H. Mittelstaedt, “The principle of reafference: Interactions between the central nervous system and the peripheral organs,” Perceptual processing: Stimulus equivalence and pattern recognition , pp. 41–72, 1971.
[9] M. Jeannerod and M. Arbib, “Action monitoring and forward control of movements,” The handbook of brain theory and neural networks , pp. 83–85, 2003.
